reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Presents as a tender, warm, erythematous, palpable cord along the course of a superficial vein, most often in the lower limb
Commonly arises in varicose veins, but can also follow intravenous cannulation or occur in otherwise normal veins
It is frequently a benign, self-limiting process, yet it should not be dismissed because it can coexist with or extend into deep vein thrombosis
Duplex ultrasound is used to confirm the diagnosis, define clot extent, and assess proximity to the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junctions and the deep system
Thrombus close to a deep junction or of substantial length carries a higher risk of propagation and venous thromboembolism, influencing whether anticoagulation is used
Management ranges from symptomatic measures for limited disease to a course of anticoagulation for extensive or junction-approaching thrombus
Migratory or recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis without varicosities should prompt consideration of an underlying thrombophilia or occult malignancy
Suppurative (septic) thrombophlebitis is a distinct infective complication requiring urgent treatment and is not the typical bland form
reference.pathophysiology: Superficial thrombophlebitis is thrombosis with accompanying inflammation of a superficial vein. The elements of Virchow's triad apply: venous stasis (notably in varicose veins), endothelial injury (for example from cannulation), and hypercoagulability. Thrombus formation within the superficial vein triggers a local inflammatory response producing the characteristic tender palpable cord. Because superficial and deep systems communicate through perforators and saphenous junctions, thrombus can propagate into the deep veins, linking the condition to venous thromboembolism.
additionalDifferentials: Contact dermatitis or insect bite reaction
additionalInvestigations: Venous duplex ultrasound to confirm diagnosis, measure clot length, and assess junctional and deep involvement
Assessment for deep vein thrombosis when clinical suspicion exists
Thrombophilia evaluation in recurrent or unprovoked cases without varicosities
Consideration of malignancy screening in migratory or recurrent disease
Review of intravenous access sites when catheter-related
redFlags: Thrombus extending toward or reaching the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junction, with risk of deep extension and pulmonary embolism
Symptoms or signs of concurrent deep vein thrombosis
Fever, purulence, or systemic upset suggesting septic (suppurative) thrombophlebitis
Migratory or recurrent phlebitis raising concern for occult malignancy or thrombophilia
reference.prognosis: Localised superficial thrombophlebitis in varicose veins is usually self-limiting with a good outcome, whereas extensive disease or thrombus near a deep junction carries a meaningful risk of progression to deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism. Recurrence is common when underlying venous disease or a prothrombotic state persists.
pitfalls: Assuming all superficial thrombophlebitis is benign and failing to assess deep or junctional extension
Mistaking it for cellulitis and treating with antibiotics alone
Overlooking an underlying malignancy or thrombophilia in migratory or recurrent cases
Not arranging duplex assessment when clot proximity to the deep system would change management
management: Manage limited disease symptomatically with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, warm compresses, compression stockings and continued mobilisation
Give anticoagulation at prophylactic intensity, such as fondaparinux or low-molecular-weight heparin, for extensive thrombus or thrombus approaching the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junction
Escalate to therapeutic anticoagulation when thrombus extends into the deep venous system, treating as for deep vein thrombosis
Remove the offending cannula when the process is catheter-related
Confirm extent and junctional proximity with duplex ultrasound and repeat imaging if there is clinical extension
Investigate for thrombophilia or occult malignancy in recurrent, migratory or unprovoked cases
Treat the underlying varicose veins once the acute episode has settled to reduce recurrence
